title: Beyond URLs: Metadata Diversity and Position for Efficient LLM Pretraining
claim: Metadata can be placed before or after each document's text in the training sequence, and this placement is the variable studied.
layout: 2 side-by-side panels, 3 stacked rows each, shared legend below
description: The figure is a schematic of how training sequences are formatted. Two side-by-side groups each show three horizontal rows of rounded blocks, standing for three sequences. In every row the first block is a small purple block, the start-of-sequence token <s>. The left group puts a mustard-yellow block next to it, followed by a long dark-gray block for the document text. This is metadata prepended before the text. The right group reverses the order. The purple block is followed by the long gray text block, and the yellow metadata block comes last, so the metadata is appended. Block widths vary slightly between rows. A legend underneath maps purple to <s>, yellow to <boc>metadata<eoc>, and gray to text. The eye goes first to the bright yellow blocks, which sit on opposite sides in the two groups.
caption: Diagram of our tokenization. Each document begins with a default beginning-of-sequence (<s>) token. For each sequence, metadata is wrapped between beginning-of-context (<boc>) and end-of-context (<eoc>). Depending on the metadata position, the metadata is prepended (illustrated on the left) or appended (illustrated on the right) to the document. If a long document split into multiple sequences, metadata is attached to each one. A 10% dropout of metadata is always performed.
abstract: Incorporating metadata in Large Language Models (LLMs) pretraining has recently emerged as a promising approach to accelerate training. However prior work highlighted only one useful signal-URLs, leaving open the question of whether other forms of metadata could yield greater benefits. In this study, we investigate a wider range of metadata types and find other types of metadata, such as fine-grained indicators of document quality that can also accelerate pretraining when prepended. We identify a common feature among effective metadata: they encode information at a finer granularity. We further introduce metadata appending as a means of improving training efficiency, where predicting an appropriate metadata as auxiliary task can help speed up pretraining. In addition, learnable meta-tokens trained with masked loss can recover part of the speedup by inducing quality-aware latent structure. Using probing, we analyze latent representations to understand how metadata shapes learning. Together, these results yield practical guidelines for integrating metadata to improve both the efficiency and effectiveness of LLM pretraining.
